strengths: Provides a principled and clear formulation of interactive information gathering with LLMs as sequential Bayesian experimental design, including detailed analysis of joint-model factorization choices.

Introduces practical innovations that address real failure modes of LLM-based information gathering, such as hypothesis filtering for historical consistency and avoiding predictive-entropy approximations of EIG.

Empirical evaluation is broad and convincing: multiple LLMs, three 20-Questions datasets, active preference elicitation, same-model and cross-model questioner/answerer settings, and an ablation against a data-estimation alternative.
Substantial and consistent performance gains over strong baselines, with careful controls to keep baselines competitive (e.g., Entropy uses the same candidate generation and joint model).
The paper is well-positioned relative to prior work and clearly articulates why prior simplifications can degrade performance, especially the conflation of EIG with predictive entropy.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported with model details, prompts, datasets, and appendices documenting design choices and experimental setup.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies on simulated LLM answerers rather than real human participants, which may not fully reflect the response distributions and subjective behavior in real interactive settings.
The method is restricted to multiple-choice questions to enable reliable entropy estimation, limiting direct applicability to open-ended or free-form conversational information gathering.
The computational cost of hypothesis generation, filtering, and EIG estimation across candidate questions is not systematically quantified, which is important for practical deployment.
Some comparisons to prior BED-for-LLM methods are indirect or adapted rather than full reimplementations, though the authors provide reasonable justification for these choices.
The paper offers limited discussion of failure cases, such as when the LLM's likelihood is poorly calibrated or when the target hypothesis space cannot be represented by samples.

strengths: Formulates interactive information gathering with LLMs as a sequential Bayesian experimental design problem and gives a clear EIG-based objective.
Identifies and empirically tests an important pitfall in prior work: using marginal predictive entropy as a proxy for EIG can substantially degrade question selection.
Introduces practical algorithmic components such as hypothesis filtering, candidate question generation, and a Rao-Blackwellized EIG estimator, with ablations isolating some design choices.
Reports consistent gains over Naive QA and Entropy baselines across multiple LLMs and three 20-Questions datasets, plus an active preference elicitation task.
Provides a thoughtful discussion of prior-likelihood versus data-estimation factorizations and their implications for LLM-based BED.
weaknesses: Evaluation is entirely simulated: the answerer and judge are LLMs, not humans, so claims about real-world interactive information gathering remain unsupported.
The empirical scope is narrow: binary 20-Questions and multiple-choice movie preference elicitation do not convincingly establish the claimed general-purpose applicability.

The belief update (sample from in-context distribution, filter for consistency, then treat survivors as uniform) is heuristic and not a proper Bayesian posterior; the EIG is therefore optimized under an ad hoc distribution, weakening the claim of a principled BED method.
Computational cost and latency are not reported, despite the method requiring many LLM calls per turn for hypothesis generation, filtering, candidate generation, and EIG estimation.
Baselines are limited to Naive QA and a predictive-entropy variant; several prior LLM-BED methods are not directly compared, and the data-estimation ablation is only run on one dataset and model.
Important implementation details, including the filtering threshold, exact prompts, and hypothesis sampling procedure, are incomplete or relegated to appendices, limiting reproducibility.
No formal significance testing is provided for the main comparisons; standard errors are reported but differences are not statistically validated.

The theoretical claim that predictive entropy is generally a poor substitute for EIG is plausible but not formally established, and the paper's broad claims outpace the evidence from two simulated tasks.

strengths: Provides a principled formulation of interactive information gathering as sequential Bayesian experimental design with LLMs, clearly connecting EIG, belief updating, and query selection.

Introduces several methodologically sound innovations: Rao-Blackwellized EIG estimator using LLM logits, prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation analysis, sample-then-filter belief update, and targeted candidate generation.
Extensive and well-structured empirical evaluation on 20 Questions across three datasets and five LLMs, plus active preference elicitation, with same and different questioner/answerer models.
Substantial and consistent improvements over strong baselines: e.g., Mistral-Large Celebrities success from 14% to 91%, and gains over predictive entropy and naive QA.
Includes useful ablations and analyses (data-estimation variant, EIG vs. predictive entropy, per-turn curves, model misspecification) that support the central claims.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies on LLM-simulated users/answerers and, in the preference task, an LLM-as-judge; this may not fully reflect human behavior and leaves open the risk of self-preference or simulation artifacts.

Computational and latency costs are not analyzed, despite BED-LLM requiring many LLM calls per turn for hypothesis generation, filtering, candidate generation, and EIG estimation; practical adoption would benefit from cost-quality trade-offs.
Several key design choices (filtering threshold, temperature, number of hypotheses/candidates, prompt wording) appear heuristic and are not systematically ablated or sensitivity-tested.
Dependence on access to logits for the EIG estimator may limit applicability to some closed models/APIs; the paper could clarify how this is handled in practice.
The comparison to prior adaptive querying methods is mostly via reimplemented baselines/ablations rather than direct head-to-head evaluation against all relevant recent methods.

strengths: Provides a principled and clearly motivated formulation of interactive information gathering with LLMs as sequential Bayesian experimental design, including a careful discussion of prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation joint-model factorizations.

Introduces concrete algorithmic components for BED-LLM: candidate question generation, a Rao-Blackwellized EIG estimator using LLM predictive distributions, and a filtering-based belief update that avoids naive in-context updating.
Empirical evaluation is broad across multiple LLMs and two task domains, with substantial gains over Naive and Split baselines on 20 Questions and improved film preference elicitation.

Ablations directly test key design choices, including non-deterministic likelihood, prior-likelihood pairing, filtering/history-consistent beliefs, and explicit EIG maximization, supporting the central claims.
Demonstrates robustness under questioner-answerer model mismatch, which is important for real-world deployment where the responder may not match the questioner model.
Reproducibility details are relatively strong, with prompts, parameters, problem-set construction, and evaluation protocols provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The evaluation is entirely LLM-based: answerers are LLM-simulated and preference elicitation uses LLM-as-judge, so it does not directly validate performance with human users or real-world responders.
The method is restricted to multiple-choice questions and requires access to reasonably calibrated token probabilities/logits, limiting applicability to free-form or high-dimensional response spaces.
Computational cost and scalability are not systematically analyzed, despite repeated LLM calls for hypothesis generation, filtering, candidate question generation, and EIG estimation.
Some per-setting gains are modest or within roughly two standard errors, though the overall empirical trend favors BED-LLM.
The belief update p_f is heuristic—filtering, diversification, and uniformization—rather than a fully Bayesian posterior, so theoretical guarantees for sequential BED optimality are limited.
No code release is mentioned, and using proprietary/closed models for key experiments may reduce full reproducibility across settings.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: enabling LLMs to adaptively gather information over multiple turns.

Provides a principled BED/EIG formulation for query selection with LLMs, including a clear discussion of prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation factorizations and the role of non-deterministic likelihoods.
Introduces a concrete algorithm, BED-LLM, with practical components such as candidate question generation, Rao-Blackwellized EIG estimation, hypothesis filtering, and diversity-promoting updates.
Reports consistent gains over Naive and Split/Entropy baselines across multiple LLM families (GPT-4o, Llama, Qwen) and two task families: 20 Questions and preference elicitation.
Includes ablations that isolate the effects of the EIG objective, belief updating, and factorization choices, and considers questioner-answerer model mismatch.
The paper is generally well written, with detailed appendix material on prompts, experimental setup, and additional design discussions.
weaknesses: The evaluation is entirely synthetic/LLM-based for a paper about user preference elicitation and information gathering: 20 Questions uses an LLM answerer, and preference elicitation uses LLM-generated user profiles and an LLM-as-judge. There is no human evaluation, so the central claims about user preferences and real-world interactive information gathering are not well supported.

The key belief-updating procedure p_f is largely heuristic: hypotheses are filtered using a fixed threshold (0.2) and then assigned a uniform distribution. This is not a Bayesian update, yet the EIG is computed under a prior-likelihood model that assumes a Bayesian-style posterior update. The resulting mismatch between the EIG objective and the actual belief-updating procedure undermines the paper's claim of a fully principled sequential BED approach.

The method is limited to multiple-choice questions with enumerable answer spaces so that conditional entropies can be calculated from logits. This conflicts with the abstract's framing of a general-purpose approach for external environments and open-ended LLM interaction. Open-ended queries, tool calls, and document retrieval are not empirically demonstrated.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work on LLM question asking and information-based query selection. The main algorithmic additions are the non-deterministic likelihood term, filtering-based belief updates, and candidate-generation heuristics; these are mostly engineering choices rather than a fundamentally new framework.

Baseline coverage is limited. Prior methods such as Wang et al., Chan et al., and post-trained LLM question-asking approaches are discussed but not directly compared. The strongest reported comparisons are Naive and an author-implemented Split/Entropy baseline, which may not fully represent the state of the art.

No statistical significance tests are reported, despite repeated-use of the same target sets and visible overlaps in some confidence intervals, especially in preference elicitation. Several gains, particularly in preference elicitation, could be within noise.

There is no analysis of computational cost or latency. BED-LLM requires many LLM calls for candidate generation, hypothesis generation, filtering, and EIG estimation, but the paper does not quantify the resulting overhead versus baselines, which is important for practical deployment.

Key hyperparameters (temperature 1.3, number of hypotheses N, number of candidate questions M, filtering threshold, number of generation-filtering cycles) are fixed without sensitivity analysis or ablation, making robustness and reproducibility unclear.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility despite the detailed prompt appendix.

strengths: Introduces a principled sequential Bayesian experimental design formulation for LLM-based adaptive information gathering, with a clear information-theoretic EIG objective.
Provides a detailed and insightful analysis of joint-model factorization for LLMs, including the trade-offs between prior-likelihood and data-estimation pairings.
The proposed belief-updating procedure with hypothesis filtering and diversity promotion is well motivated and shown to be important through ablations.
Empirical results are strong and broad: BED-LLM substantially outperforms Naive, Split/Entropy, and other ablations across multiple LLMs on 20 Questions, and also improves preference elicitation.
Demonstrates robustness to questioner-answerer model mismatch, which is important for real-world applicability.
Reproducibility is well supported with prompts, algorithmic details, datasets, and evaluation protocols in the appendix.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to simulated LLM answerers rather than human users, so external validity for real interactive settings remains uncertain.
Preference-elicitation gains are sometimes modest and overlap with error bars for some model pairs; no formal significance tests are reported.
Computational cost and LLM-call overhead are not quantified, which matters for practical deployment given the many hypotheses, candidate questions, and likelihood evaluations.
The preference-elicitation evaluation relies on LLM-as-judge scoring, which may introduce bias and noise despite consistency checks.
The Data-Estimation ablation cannot be run for GPT models due to API log-probability limitations, leaving that comparison incomplete for half of the evaluated model families.
Some hyperparameters, such as the filtering threshold and diversity-promotion settings, appear fixed and are not extensively ablated, so sensitivity is unclear.
